title: Failure Propagation — What Happens When One Node Dies

questions.prompt: Graph: build → tests → release, and build → docs. The tests node fails. Which nodes can still run, and which are tainted?
options: Everything stops; a failure is fatal to the graph
Docs and its descendants can still run; release is tainted because tests is its ancestor
Release can run, because only tests failed
Nothing can run until tests is retried to success
questions.explanation: A failure taints the failed node's descendants (release), not sibling branches that never depended on it (docs). Option A is the tempting "fail the whole run" reflex and throws away independent work. Option C ignores that release consumes tests' output. Option D blocks independent branches on a node they do not need.

questions.prompt: A node charges a customer and then, on a transient network error, retries three times. The customer is charged three times. What property was missing?
options: A longer lease on the claim
Idempotency — a retry must not double-apply its side effect
A soft edge between charge and retry
Fail-open, so the run continues past the error
questions.explanation: Bounded retries are only safe if re-running a node does not repeat its side effect; a charge needs a dedupe key or a check-before-write. Option A addresses who owns the node, not repeated effects. Option C is an edge-classification idea and unrelated. Option D would proceed on error, which here means shipping a triple charge.

questions.prompt: A lint node fails. A team decides this should stop the whole release. Identify the mistake and the fix.
options: No mistake — lint failures should always block
A harmless advisory node is fail-closed and is gating work it should not; make it fail-open with a recorded marker unless the lint is a hard gate
The lint node should have no failure definition at all
The lint node needs a longer retry bound
questions.explanation: Fail-open versus fail-closed is chosen per node for its consequence; a lint is advisory unless it enforces a rule the team treats as blocking. Option A is the tempting "stricter is safer," which serialises shipping on a cosmetic check. Option C removes verification entirely. Option D retries a deterministic failure, which cannot fix it.

questions.prompt: A worker is killed after claiming a node but before finishing. The runner reports the graph complete, yet the node's descendant never ran. What two mechanisms were missing?
options: A broader fan-out and a smaller lease
Orphan detection via lease expiry, and propagation so the descendants are marked rather than silently skipped
A soft edge and an interface
A decision node and a spike
questions.explanation: The claim's lease must expire so the node is retried or failed, and the failure must propagate so the descendant is not quietly omitted. Option A widens the problem without adding recovery or reporting. Options C and D are concepts from Lessons 100 and 102 that do not address a dead owner or a lost descendant.
